summary: This document discusses using only link-local addresses on infrastructure links between routers in an IPv6 network. It weighs the advantages and disadvantages to help operators decide.

eli5.summary: Routers next to each other can talk using local-only addresses. This RFC lists the good and bad sides of doing that.

subtitle: Using only local addresses on router infrastructure links

tldr.problem: Router infrastructure links traditionally carry globally routable IPv6 addresses, which enlarges routing tables and creates more targets for attack.
tldr.mechanism: This approach uses only link-local addresses on infrastructure links between routers and global addresses only on loopback interfaces, reducing the attack surface and routing table size.
tldr.outcome: The technique has real benefits in some networks (smaller tables, simpler management) but introduces operational challenges for troubleshooting and some advanced routing scenarios.

today: RFC 7404 is an Informational document. It describes an approach that some operators use and others do not. The document makes no recommendation but documents the trade-offs clearly, allowing operators to make informed decisions for their environments.

sections.title: Using Link-Local Addresses on Infrastructure
sections.content:
In traditional IPv6 networks, links between routers carry global or unique local addresses, even though routers do not typically receive traffic from outside the network destined for those link addresses. Using only link-local addresses (starting with fe80::) on these infrastructure links offers several operational and security benefits.

Link-local addresses are automatically configured on every IPv6 interface and are not routable beyond the link. Routing protocols like BGP, OSPF, and IS-IS can work with link-local addresses for neighbor communication. This document explores the advantages and disadvantages of this approach to help network operators evaluate it for their deployments.
sections.eli5: Links between routers only need addresses that work between those two routers. Using local-only addresses keeps these links hidden from the broader internet.

sections.title: Advantages of Link-Local Only Approach
sections.content:
Smaller routing tables: Since the routing protocol only needs to carry one loopback address per router instead of every infrastructure link address, routing tables are smaller. This reduces memory, speeds up routing convergence, and lets line cards download a smaller Forwarding Information Base.

Simpler address management: Only loopback addresses need to be included in address planning. This makes renumbering simpler and reduces operational overhead.

Lower configuration complexity: Link-local addresses require no manual configuration, and address errors are nearly impossible. Routing protocols handle neighbor discovery automatically.

Reduced attack surface: Infrastructure links are not reachable from outside the network, preventing remote attacks targeting those addresses. Attackers can only compromise the loopback addresses if they gain network access.
sections.eli5: Fewer routable addresses means smaller routing tables, easier to manage, fewer mistakes, and fewer things for attackers to target from outside the network.

sections.title: Challenges and Limitations
sections.content:
Interface troubleshooting: Traditional tools like ping and traceroute do not work on infrastructure interfaces with only link-local addresses. Operators must use alternative methods like pinging loopback addresses or connecting via SSH for local checks. RFC 5837 provides some solutions by allowing ICMP responses to include interface identifiers.

Hardware changes: Link-local addresses are typically based on the MAC address, so replacing a line card changes the address. This breaks BGP neighbor relationships. Static link-local configuration (fe80::1, fe80::2) solves this but requires explicit zone indices.

Network management tools: Tools using interface IP addresses may not work. Workarounds include configuring management systems to use loopback addresses or using protocols like LLDP that do not depend on IP addresses.

MPLS/RSVP-TE limitations: RSVP-TE explicit path setup cannot use link-local addresses. Networks using Fast Reroute must keep global addresses on infrastructure links.
sections.eli5: Network engineers lose some useful tools for checking if links work. Some advanced routing features cannot work with local-only addresses.

sections.title: Special Considerations for Internet Exchange Points
sections.content:
Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) present a unique security challenge. IXP infrastructure prefix addresses are publicly discoverable and practically all routers on the prefix are critical Internet infrastructure, making them attractive targets. Using link-local addresses means ICMP error messages originate from each service provider's own address space rather than the IXP prefix, complicating potential attacks.

However, an attacker can still discover IXP loopback addresses via traceroute. Some operators benefit from hiding the IXP prefix by using link-local addresses, while others need to carry IXP addresses in their Interior Gateway Protocol for traffic engineering purposes.
sections.eli5: Large internet connection points have special concerns about attackers discovering their addresses. Using local addresses helps hide the infrastructure but makes some traffic management harder.

sections.title: Making the Decision
sections.content:
The RFC documents both advantages and disadvantages without recommending for or against this approach. Network operators should evaluate whether link-local-only addressing suits their specific environment, constraints, and operational practices.

The technique works best in networks that do not use RSVP-TE for explicit paths, have good out-of-band or loopback-based management practices, and prioritize routing table size and attack surface reduction. It may not suit networks heavily dependent on interface-level ping testing or those requiring advanced traffic engineering on infrastructure links.
sections.eli5: Different networks have different needs. Some benefit from local-only addressing, while others need full addresses for troubleshooting or advanced features.
